paragraphs: Learning-to-optimize trains algorithms to carry out optimization more effectively. Although these learned algorithms can deliver substantial empirical improvements, their convergence is harder to justify theoretically. Classical convergence proofs often depend on geometric properties of the optimization process, and those arguments do not transfer easily to algorithms whose behavior is learned.

The paper develops a probabilistic framework that retains enough of the structure of classical optimization to reuse geometric reasoning. Its new proof strategy supports a generalization theorem for parameterized families of loss functions, including losses that may be non-smooth or non-convex. The theorem establishes convergence of learned optimization algorithms to critical points with high probability.

This provides a way to connect learned optimization behavior with mathematical convergence guarantees beyond the cases directly analyzed during design. The result concerns critical points rather than a claim of finding globally optimal solutions. By recasting worst-case reasoning probabilistically, the framework also allows learned algorithms to be designed without the safeguards that would otherwise constrain their construction.
icml-2025-a-generalization-result-for-co.tldr: A probabilistic framework establishes high-probability convergence to critical points for learned optimizers across parameterized loss families.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adapters, or LoRAs, make foundation-model fine-tuning more economical by representing a matrix through two smaller matrices. Combining several LoRA adapters as a mixture of experts can increase their expressive capacity. However, the paper identifies weaknesses in the robustness of these mixtures during both tuning and inference, despite their improvements on downstream tasks.

The proposed training strategy draws on Riemannian preconditioning, which treats a LoRA adapter as a projection into a subspace. It extends this perspective to several experts through gate-rescaled multi-space projections. In plain terms, the method changes how the experts learn across their respective spaces while accounting for the gates that determine their contributions.

The authors provide both a theoretical solution and an alternative engineering strategy for applying the idea. Evaluations with SGD and AdamW support the effectiveness of the approach. The contribution is therefore a way to stabilize and strengthen feature learning in mixtures of low-rank adapters, addressing how those adapters are trained as well as how much representational capacity they provide.
icml-2025-a-stronger-mixture-of-low-rank.tldr: Gate-rescaled projections improve the stability and feature learning of mixtures of low-rank adapters.

paragraphs: Prediction systems often receive features that are missing, incorrectly observed, or only partially available. Methods can estimate the underlying feature values before using them for a downstream prediction, but separate treatments of different defects make their behavior difficult to compare. This paper introduces Weak Features Learning, a framework that accommodates arbitrary discrete weak features and a broad range of algorithms.

Within this framework, the authors introduce a class of methods that learn both a feature-estimation model and a downstream prediction model. Their finite-sample analysis studies how errors in reconstructing the inputs interact with errors in the final prediction. This connects the two learning problems instead of evaluating feature recovery in isolation.

The results also identify theoretical conditions necessary for consistency, addressing when the learning approach can approach its intended target as data increases. The contribution is a common foundation for analyzing varied forms of discrete input uncertainty. Its guarantees explain the dependence between feature quality and prediction performance rather than assuming that estimating weak features automatically produces reliable downstream predictions.
icml-2025-a-unified-framework-for-genera.tldr: A unified framework analyzes how estimation errors in arbitrary discrete weak features affect downstream prediction and consistency.

paragraphs: Graphs can contain different kinds of structure, including hierarchies and more evenly distributed relationships. Different geometric spaces offer different advantages for representing these patterns. Combining geometries has helped with static graphs, but predicting relationships in evolving systems also requires representing how nodes and connections change over time.

The paper proposes a unified framework that combines Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces for dynamic graphs. It models fine-grained substructures so that the embedding geometry can align with the structure being represented. A temporal state aggregation mechanism brings together information over time, while an evolution-driven optimization objective directs learning toward changes in both nodes and relationships.

These components link structural representation with temporal modeling within one learning framework. Experiments on multiple real-world dynamic graph datasets report improvements over existing methods across several metrics. The findings support the value of adapting geometry to local graph structure while explicitly accounting for evolution, rather than relying only on representations developed for a fixed snapshot.
icml-2025-analytical-construction-on-geo.tldr: A dynamic graph framework combines Euclidean and hyperbolic representations with temporal modeling to improve link prediction.

paragraphs: Video diffusion transformers can produce high-quality videos, but their computation is expensive. AsymRnR targets that cost without additional training. Its starting observation is that feature-token redundancy varies across model blocks, denoising steps, and feature types. Consequently, different parts of the generation process offer different opportunities to reduce attention computation.

The method removes redundant tokens asymmetrically within attention rather than applying the same reduction everywhere. A tailored schedule distributes reduction adaptively across components, reflecting the uneven redundancy the authors observe. A matching cache further accelerates the reduction process, addressing the overhead involved in deciding which tokens can be reduced.

The authors describe the approach as model-agnostic and demonstrate integration into leading video diffusion transformers. Their theoretical treatment and experiments support substantial acceleration with negligible deterioration in output quality; some cases even show quality improvements. These findings suggest that selectively reducing attention work can make video generation faster while preserving the information needed for good outputs in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-asymrnr-video-diffusion-transf.tldr: AsymRnR accelerates video diffusion transformers without training by adaptively reducing redundant attention tokens.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing provides certified guarantees against adversarial perturbations, and average certified radius is commonly used to compare its progress. This paper argues that the average can give a misleading picture of robustness. A model can improve the metric by concentrating on easy examples while becoming less robust on difficult ones.

The authors prove that even a trivial classifier can have an arbitrarily large average certified radius. They also show that the metric is highly sensitive to gains on easy samples and that comparisons depend strongly on the certification budget. Empirical results find that existing training strategies can raise the average while consistently reducing robustness on hard samples.

To demonstrate the problem directly, the paper explores discarding hard examples, reweighting data, and aggressively optimizing easy examples. These strategies can reproduce reported progress and reach state-of-the-art average certified radius on CIFAR-10 without training for robustness across the full distribution. The authors recommend abandoning this metric and propose examining the empirical distribution of the base model’s accuracy on noisy inputs instead.
icml-2025-average-certified-radius-is-a-.tldr: Average certified radius can reward gains on easy examples while concealing weaker robustness on hard examples.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised semantic segmentation uses unlabeled images to help learn pixel-level predictions. A central decision is which model-generated labels to trust during training. Confidence thresholds provide one signal, but accepting more useful labels can also admit more incorrect ones. The paper seeks a better balance by adding information from learned feature representations.

The authors construct clean reference sets of correct and incorrect pseudo labels, called positive and negative agents. Their Agent Score, or AgScore, measures agreement between candidate pixels and these sets. It uses patterns in embedding space while conditioning on agents obtained from prediction space, retaining the benefits of confidence information and adding evidence about feature similarity.

The paper provides theoretical analysis of this scoring mechanism and tests it within three semi-supervised segmentation frameworks. Evaluations on Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, and COCO show consistent improvements across all tested data partitions. The results support using structured agreement with positive and negative references to improve pseudo-label selection, making unlabeled data more useful for the downstream segmentation task.
icml-2025-beyond-confidence-exploiting-h.tldr: AgScore improves pseudo-label selection for segmentation by combining confidence information with agreement against positive and negative feature references.

paragraphs: Model merging aims to combine several task-specific experts into one model without additional training. A common approach adds task vectors, the parameter changes between a pretrained model and its fine-tuned versions. However, changes that help one task can conflict with changes from another, causing the merged model to lose performance.

Conflict-Aware Task Merging, or CAT Merging, selectively trims components of those vectors that are prone to conflict. It treats parameter types differently: linear weights use projection, while normalization-layer scaling and shifting parameters use masking. This makes conflict handling sensitive to the role of the parameters being combined instead of applying one uniform operation.

Experiments on vision and vision-language tasks indicate that these strategies suppress conflicts effectively. The authors report average accuracy improvements of up to 4.7% for ViT-B/32 and 2.0% for ViT-L/14 over state-of-the-art methods. The findings show that carefully selecting which parts of task-specific updates to retain can improve a merged model while preserving a training-free workflow.
icml-2025-cat-merging-a-training-free-ap.tldr: CAT Merging improves training-free model merging by trimming conflicting task updates with parameter-specific operations.

paragraphs: Sparse tensor programs appear in deep learning and graph analytics, but optimizing them for new accelerators is difficult. Their speed depends strongly on the particular sparse inputs. Meanwhile, early accelerator development often depends on expensive simulators, making it costly to collect enough performance measurements to train a useful optimization cost model.

COGNATE first trains cost models using inexpensive samples from general-purpose hardware such as CPUs, then adapts them with a small amount of data from the emerging hardware. The framework uses similarities in input features across platforms while accounting for hardware differences. This makes information gathered on an accessible machine useful for optimization on a less accessible accelerator.

The authors report comparable cost-model performance using just 5% of the samples required by accelerator-specific models. Their experiments also show average speedups of 1.47 times for SpMM and 1.39 times for SDDMM, with maxima of 5.46 and 4.22 times. These results connect reduced training-data requirements with improvements in the execution speed of the optimized sparse programs.
icml-2025-cognate-acceleration-of-sparse.tldr: COGNATE transfers cost models from general-purpose hardware to emerging accelerators, reducing data needs and accelerating sparse tensor programs.

paragraphs: Directed acyclic graphs represent structures such as electronic circuits, Bayesian networks, and neural architectures. Turning these graphs into sequences is attractive for learning, but a single graph can admit many valid topological node orders. That ambiguity complicates the task of decoding a sequence into a graph in a principled way.

The paper proposes representing a graph as a derivation under an unambiguous grammar. Each DAG corresponds to a unique sequence of production rules, giving a compact sequential description that preserves the graph. The authors also interpret this construction as lossless compression: the sequence provides an equivalent representation rather than discarding structural information to simplify the input.

This representation can support several kinds of learning over structured objects. The paper identifies graph generation, property prediction through a learned latent space, and Bayesian optimization as uses. For optimization, continuity in the sequential representation provides a way to work with structured candidates. The central contribution is a common, unambiguous description that connects DAG structure with sequence-based modeling.
icml-2025-directed-graph-grammars-for-se.tldr: An unambiguous graph grammar gives each DAG a unique, lossless sequence representation for learning and generation.

paragraphs: Vision-language models learn visual representations partly through text supervision, but text carries less detailed information than the images it describes. The paper also identifies information loss during gradient propagation as a weakness in that supervision. Together, these issues can limit how effectively language-based learning shapes the model’s visual features.

DS-VLM adds direct supervision through a diffusion model that reconstructs input images. Reconstruction is conditioned on outputs from the visual encoder and the connector, creating a shorter route for pixel-level learning signals to reach visual features. Conventional text supervision remains in place, so the framework combines semantic alignment with constraints derived from reconstructing the image itself.

This division gives the two supervision sources complementary roles: text maintains high-level meaning, while reconstruction strengthens visual feature quality. The authors describe DS-VLM as a plug-and-play framework and evaluate it with several visual encoders and language models of different sizes. Their experiments support its effectiveness across these configurations, indicating that diffusion-based image reconstruction can usefully supplement language supervision.
icml-2025-ds-vlm-diffusion-supervision-v.tldr: DS-VLM supplements text supervision with diffusion-based image reconstruction to improve visual features and vision-language alignment.

paragraphs: Quantization makes large language models smaller and faster by representing values with lower precision. Outliers make this difficult when the available quantization points are evenly spaced. FlatQuant starts from the observation that existing transformations can still leave weight and activation distributions steep and dispersed, allowing substantial quantization error to remain.

The method learns an affine transformation for each linear layer to flatten those distributions before quantization. It uses a lightweight calibration objective, with calibration completed in hours. To keep the transformations inexpensive during inference, the authors express them through a Kronecker product of two lightweight matrices and combine the operations into a single kernel.

Experiments report less than a 1% accuracy drop for four-bit weights and activations on LLaMA-3-70B, outperforming SpinQuant by 7.5%. FlatQuant also achieves up to 2.3 times faster prefill and 1.7 times faster decoding than the FP16 model. These findings show that distribution shaping and efficient implementation can work together to improve the practical value of post-training quantization.
icml-2025-flatquant-flatness-matters-for.tldr: FlatQuant learns efficient transformations that flatten model values, improving low-precision accuracy and inference speed.

paragraphs: Multimodal person re-identification seeks to match observations of a person across different forms of input. Existing approaches often support only limited combinations of query and retrieval modalities, which restricts deployment. FlexiReID addresses this inflexibility with a framework supporting seven retrieval modes across RGB images, infrared images, sketches, and text.

Its adaptive mixture-of-experts mechanism dynamically combines features from different modalities. A cross-modal query fusion module further improves extraction of information from multimodal queries. Together, these components give the framework a way to account for diverse input types when constructing the representations used for matching, within the retrieval modes it supports.

The authors also introduce CIRS-PEDES, a unified dataset that extends four established person re-identification datasets to include all four modalities. This provides a shared setting for evaluating the broader retrieval capability. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization in complex scenarios. The contribution combines a more flexible matching framework with evaluation data designed to cover its multimodal scope.
icml-2025-flexireid-adaptive-mixture-of-.tldr: FlexiReID uses adaptive experts and query fusion to support seven person-retrieval modes across four modalities.

paragraphs: Online platforms use discounts and coupons to encourage engagement, and uplift models estimate responses to these incentives from observational data. Such estimates face selection bias, but they must also cope with users changing across time, geography, and other conditions. Testing only on data that resembles training can miss this second challenge.

Invariant Deep Uplift Modeling, or IDUM, seeks causal factors that remain consistent across domains to improve generalization outside the training distribution. It further refines these into necessary and sufficient factors. A masking component selects informative invariant features to reduce computational cost, while a balancing discrepancy component addresses selection bias in the observational data.

The framework therefore treats changing user populations and biased observations as related challenges requiring distinct mechanisms. Experiments on public and real-world datasets support effectiveness both within and outside the training distribution. The authors also provide theoretical analysis and proofs supporting generalizability. The stated findings suggest that stable causal features can help incentive-response models remain useful as the conditions around an online marketing platform change.
icml-2025-invariant-deep-uplift-modeling.tldr: IDUM combines invariant causal features and bias balancing to improve incentive-response modeling across changing user distributions.

paragraphs: Denoising generative models are commonly given information about the noise level they are handling. This paper questions whether that explicit conditioning is indispensable for successful generation. Inspired by blind image denoising, the authors investigate what happens when a variety of denoising-based generative models operate without noise conditioning.

Most models in their investigation deteriorate gradually rather than failing outright, and some perform better without the conditioning information. The authors also mathematically analyze the error introduced by removing it. That analysis agrees with their empirical observations, giving a theoretical account alongside the experiments rather than relying only on the surprising outcomes.

The paper further introduces a model without noise conditioning that reaches an FID of 2.23 on CIFAR-10, narrowing the gap to leading noise-conditioned models. The findings challenge a necessity claim: explicit noise information is not essential for every successful denoising generator examined here. They do not imply that removing conditioning improves every model, since the reported behavior includes both degradation and occasional improvement.
icml-2025-is-noise-conditioning-necessar.tldr: Experiments and analysis show that many denoising generators remain effective without explicit noise conditioning.

paragraphs: Self-attention handles long contexts effectively but has quadratic complexity, while recurrent layers offer linear complexity with less expressive hidden states. This paper proposes making the hidden state itself a machine learning model. Updating that state becomes a self-supervised learning step, allowing the sequence layer to adapt its internal model as it reads.

These Test-Time Training layers continue updating on test sequences, which gives the approach its name. The authors study TTT-Linear, whose state is a linear model, and TTT-MLP, whose state is a two-layer neural network. Both instantiate a framework intended to combine linear sequence-processing complexity with a richer form of recurrent memory.

Evaluations from 125 million to 1.3 billion parameters compare the layers with a strong Transformer and Mamba. Both TTT variants continue reducing perplexity with additional context, similarly to the Transformer, whereas Mamba stops benefiting beyond 16,000 tokens in these evaluations. TTT-MLP shows greater long-context potential but still encounters memory input/output challenges, distinguishing its modeling promise from its implementation efficiency.
icml-2025-learning-to-learn-at-test-time.tldr: Test-Time Training layers use a learnable model as recurrent memory, enabling continued benefits from longer context with linear complexity.

paragraphs: Low-precision training can reduce training and inference costs, but floating-point precision involves more than a single bit count. The paper studies how quantization targets, exponent bits, mantissa bits, and scaling-factor granularity affect language-model performance. It argues that scaling laws centered on integer quantization do not adequately capture these floating-point choices.

The authors develop a unified scaling law for floating-point quantization and derive guidance for allocating bits. Their findings indicate that exponent bits contribute slightly more to performance than mantissa bits, and they provide preferred ratios for different total precisions. They also identify a critical training-data size beyond which additional data degrades performance in the low-precision setting they analyze.

The resulting picture links numerical format, dataset size, and available computation rather than treating precision as an isolated setting. The authors report that optimal precision grows with computational power and estimate that four to eight bits offers the best cost-performance balance over a broad compute range. This is a scaling-based estimate, with the recommended precision tied to the computational setting.
icml-2025-scaling-laws-for-floatingpoint.tldr: A floating-point scaling law connects bit allocation, data size, and compute, estimating a broad cost-performance sweet spot at four to eight bits.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can learn complex behavior from demonstrations, including behavior requiring precise control and long-term planning. Their robustness can weaken when encountered conditions differ from the demonstrations. This paper studies how online interaction with the environment can improve these imitation-learned policies through reinforcement learning.

The proposed OTPR method connects diffusion policies with reinforcement learning using optimal transport. It uses the Q-function as a transport cost and interprets the policy as a transport map, providing a basis for efficient, stable fine-tuning. Masked optimal transport guides state-action matching with expert keypoints, while compatibility-based resampling adds another mechanism for stabilizing training.

Experiments on three simulation tasks report better performance and robustness than existing methods, particularly in complex settings and environments with sparse rewards. The results support optimal transport as a practical connection between demonstrated behavior and reward-driven adaptation. The contribution is a fine-tuning framework that allows diffusion policies to build on imitation learning through environmental feedback, with the reported evidence coming from the simulated tasks.
icml-2025-score-based-diffusion-policy-c.tldr: OTPR uses optimal transport to fine-tune diffusion policies with reinforcement learning, improving robustness on three simulated tasks.

paragraphs: Long-context language models retain a growing key-value cache during generation. Both storing that cache and accessing it for each decoding step can reduce serving throughput. Sparse attention can reduce work, but existing methods may leave too much data on the GPU or introduce substantial delays when moving cached data from the CPU.

ShadowKV combines a low-rank key cache with an offloaded value cache to reduce GPU memory requirements. Its selection strategy reconstructs a small set of sparse key-value pairs as needed, aiming to limit decoding latency. The memory savings allow larger batches and longer sequences, while selective reconstruction addresses the cost of retrieving the relevant context.

Evaluations include RULER, LongBench, Llama-3.1-8B, and GLM-4-9B-1M. On an A100 GPU, the authors report up to six times larger batches and 3.04 times higher throughput without sacrificing accuracy. They also report exceeding a comparison with infinite batch size under an infinite-GPU-memory assumption, showing that the claimed throughput benefit extends beyond simply fitting more requests into memory.
icml-2025-shadowkv-kv-cache-in-shadows-f.tldr: ShadowKV combines compact key storage, value offloading, and selective reconstruction to improve long-context inference throughput.

paragraphs: Panoramic image outpainting completes missing visual content for immersive scenes. Its geometry differs from ordinary planar images because the content represents a sphere. Existing panoramic approaches encourage spherical behavior through soft regularization during learning, but the paper argues that this does not fully use the structure of panoramic content.

Spherical-nested diffusion, or SpND, incorporates that geometry into the diffusion model’s design. Spherical noise supplies a structural prior during the diffusion process, and a spherical deformable convolution module learns panoramic information. These components make the spherical format part of the learning mechanism, and the resulting method can be integrated into a pretrained diffusion model.

The authors report outperforming existing panoramic outpainting methods, including an FID reduction of more than 50% relative to PanoDiffusion. This provides empirical support for building the target geometry into generation rather than depending only on a training penalty to encourage it. The contribution links a representation-specific model design with improved panoramic completion in the reported evaluation.
icml-2025-spherical-nested-diffusion-mod.tldr: SpND builds spherical structure into diffusion-based panoramic outpainting and reports more than a 50% FID reduction over PanoDiffusion.

paragraphs: Combining images from different modalities can preserve complementary information, but real inputs often contain damage. Visible images may suffer from noise, blur, or haze, while infrared images can contain stripe noise. TG-ECNet addresses the need to restore these inputs and fuse their information within a single system.

Its task-aware gating operates in two stages. Degradation-aware gates assign restoration work to expert groups according to the type of degradation. Fusion-aware gates then guide the integration of features across modalities, balancing information retention between restoration and fusion. A two-stage training strategy brings the two tasks together and addresses their conflicting information-processing requirements.

Experiments show improved fusion performance under varied, complex degradation conditions and stronger robustness in downstream applications. The result matters because cleaning an image and preserving useful information from several modalities are connected but different objectives. By coordinating specialized restoration experts with fusion-aware integration, the framework supports an all-in-one process whose reported benefits extend beyond the fused image to its later use.
icml-2025-task-gated-multi-expert-collab.tldr: TG-ECNet coordinates restoration experts and multimodal fusion through task-aware gates to handle degraded images.

paragraphs: When benchmark questions appear in language-model training data, test scores can overstate capability. Researchers try to mitigate this contamination by modifying questions or generating replacements. This paper examines whether those changes both resist contamination and preserve the evaluation behavior of the original benchmark.

The authors build a controlled assessment pipeline with two metrics: fidelity and contamination resistance. Both emphasize matching evaluation outcomes at the question level, addressing information that aggregate accuracy comparisons can hide. Their experiments cover 10 language models, five benchmarks, 20 mitigation strategies, and two contamination scenarios, allowing them to examine the tradeoff across many tested configurations.

No tested strategy effectively balances the two objectives. Strategies that preserve semantics do not significantly improve contamination resistance over unchanged benchmarks across all five benchmarks, while strategies that alter semantics gain resistance at the expense of fidelity. The findings question whether updating benchmark questions reliably fixes contamination: an update may either leave the problem insufficiently addressed or change what the evaluation is measuring.
icml-2025-the-emperors-new-clothes-in-be.tldr: A controlled study finds that tested benchmark updates fail to balance contamination resistance with fidelity to the original evaluation.

paragraphs: An infinite-armed bandit models decision-making with an unlimited supply of possible actions, whose initial mean rewards come from a reservoir distribution. When rewards change over time, selecting good actions becomes harder. Previous optimal regret guarantees required knowledge of non-stationarity parameters and applied only under particular regularity conditions on that reservoir.

This paper establishes parameter-free optimal regret bounds while relaxing those distributional assumptions. It also develops a notion of significant shifts, aiming to characterize the changes that meaningfully affect the decision problem. The authors show that algorithms can adaptively attain tighter regret bounds expressed through these significant shifts.

A notable feature of the enhanced rates is that they depend only on rotting, or decreasing, rewards. Rising rewards do not contribute to the non-stationarity difficulty measured by these bounds. This distinguishes the direction of reward changes within the analysis rather than treating every fluctuation as equally costly. The result provides a sharper account of adaptation while removing the need for advance parameter knowledge.
icml-2025-tracking-most-significant-shif.tldr: Parameter-free bandit guarantees adapt to significant reward shifts, with enhanced rates depending on decreases rather than increases.

paragraphs: Weak features are inputs degraded by missing values, measurement errors, or ambiguous observations. Learning from them involves both estimating useful feature information and predicting the downstream label. Earlier theory addressed discrete weak features, but its reliance on discreteness prevents a direct extension to continuous inputs.

The paper develops a formal framework and error analysis specifically for continuous weak features. It captures the interaction between the feature-estimation model and the label-prediction model, placing both parts of the learning process within one analysis. The authors also derive conditions necessary for consistency for sequential and iterative learning methods.

These results explain what must hold for the two types of learning procedure to achieve consistency when the uncertain inputs are continuous. Combined with existing discrete-feature theory, the framework covers both discrete and continuous forms of weak features. Its contribution is a broader theoretical foundation for understanding how feature recovery and downstream prediction fit together, including applications involving missing data, rather than treating input estimation as an independent preprocessing concern.
icml-2025-unified-analysis-of-continuous.tldr: A continuous weak-feature framework analyzes estimation–prediction interactions and necessary conditions for sequential and iterative learning consistency.

paragraphs: Online linear programming supports decisions in resource allocation and revenue management as information arrives. Repeatedly solving linear programs can achieve low regret, but those solves are computationally expensive. First-order methods are cheaper to run, yet typically offer weaker regret guarantees. This paper combines the two approaches to improve that tradeoff.

The algorithm re-solves a linear-programming subproblem periodically using a predefined frequency parameter f. The latest dual prices guide online decisions. Between these solves, a first-order method runs in parallel and smooths resource consumption, allowing decisions to continue while the more expensive optimization is performed less frequently.

The authors establish regret of order log(T/f) plus the square root of f, connecting the performance guarantee to the re-solving schedule and decision horizon. Experiments report at least tenfold improvements in regret over first-order methods and hundredfold improvements in runtime over LP-based methods. These findings support combining periodic optimization with inexpensive ongoing updates to obtain efficient online decisions without giving up strong regret control.
icml-2025-wait-less-offline-tuning-and-r.tldr: Periodic linear-program solves combined with first-order updates improve the tradeoff between online decision quality and computational cost.
